Death & the Afterlife

Religious beliefs about what happens after death influence attitudes towards euthanasia and the value of life.

Christianity: Most Christians believe in an afterlife. The soul continues after death — the righteous go to heaven (eternal life with God) and the unrighteous face judgement. Jesus said: “I am the resurrection and the life. The one who believes in me will live, even though they die” (John 11:25). This belief gives Christians hope and comfort in the face of death.

Islam: Muslims believe in Yawm al-Din (the Day of Judgement), when Allah will resurrect all people and judge their deeds. The righteous will enter Jannah (paradise) and the wicked will be sent to Jahannam (hell). This belief means Muslims see life as a test and believe suffering has a purpose — it builds patience and strengthens faith.

Belief in an afterlife reinforces opposition to euthanasia. If this life is a preparation for eternal life, then cutting it short may have spiritual consequences. Christians may fear that taking one’s own life or assisting death goes against God’s plan. Muslims believe that accepting suffering patiently is rewarded in the afterlife. However, some non-religious people argue that without an afterlife, reducing suffering in this life becomes even more important — supporting the case for euthanasia.

Key Fact

Humanists and atheists, who do not believe in an afterlife, argue that moral decisions should focus on reducing suffering in this life. They may support euthanasia because they believe people have the right to die with dignity. This contrasts with religious views that see suffering as meaningful and life as belonging to God.
replace: Beliefs about life after death also shape how people value life now. Christians and Muslims believe that this life is given by God and prepares a person for what comes next, so ending a life early is a serious step. That belief strengthens the sanctity of life argument against abortion and euthanasia. Christian, Muslim and non-religious beliefs about death and the afterlife are taught in full in the lesson on death and an afterlife.

find: Arguments for: People should have the right to choose how and when they die. Forcing someone to live in extreme pain is cruel. Quality of life matters — when there is no hope of recovery, euthanasia may be the most compassionate option. Some argue Jesus’s Golden Rule (“Do to others what you would have them do to you” — Matthew 7:12) supports ending suffering.
replace: Arguments for: Humanists and other non-religious people argue that a person should be able to choose how and when they die, and that dying with dignity matters. Forcing someone to live in extreme pain is cruel. Quality of life matters — when there is no hope of recovery, euthanasia may be the most compassionate option. Some Christians argue that Jesus’s Golden Rule (“Do to others what you would have them do to you” — Matthew 7:12) supports ending suffering.

expect.text: Explain two similar religious beliefs about what happens after death. In your answer you should refer to the main religious tradition of Great Britain and one or more other religious traditions.
expect.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per belief (1 for stating, 2 for developing):
• Christians believe in an afterlife / the righteous go to heaven / Jesus said 'I am the resurrection and the life. The one who believes in me will live, even though they die' (John 11:25).
• Muslims believe in Yawm al-Din (Day of Judgement) / Allah will judge everyone’s deeds / the righteous enter Jannah (paradise) and the wicked face Jahannam (hell).
• Both religions teach that this life is a preparation for eternal life and that moral behaviour in this life determines what happens after death.

value.text: Explain two contrasting beliefs in contemporary British society about euthanasia. In your answer you should refer to the main religious tradition of Great Britain and one or more other religious traditions.
value.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per belief (1 for stating, 2 for developing):
• Most Christians believe euthanasia is wrong because life is a gift from God / only God should decide when life ends / Job 1:21 says 'The Lord gave and the Lord has taken away' / palliative care relieves suffering without hastening death.
• Muslims believe only Allah decides the time of death / 'No soul can die except by Allah’s leave' (Qur’an 3:145) / suffering is to be borne patiently because 'Allah does not burden a soul beyond that it can bear' (2:286).
• Contrasting view within Christianity: some Christians apply Jesus’s Golden Rule (Matthew 7:12) and argue that ending extreme suffering is the most loving choice. Humanists argue that a person should be able to choose the time of their own death.
